clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive ataxia caused by biallelic SYNE1 mutations affecting nesprin-1, a component of the LINC complex that tethers the nuclear envelope to the cytoskeleton.
Originally described as a relatively pure, adult-onset, slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia in a French-Canadian population (the recessive ataxia of Beauce).
Dysarthria is common and often prominent, accompanying gait and limb ataxia and cerebellar oculomotor signs such as nystagmus and saccadic pursuit.

Beyond the pure cerebellar form, an expanded multisystem phenotype includes upper and lower motor neuron signs, brainstem involvement and occasional cognitive change, reported more often outside Quebec.
Brain MRI typically shows cerebellar atrophy, with relative preservation of other structures in the pure form.
SYNE1 is an exceptionally large gene, and distinct mutations underlie different disorders including arthrogryposis and Emery-Dreifuss-like presentations.
Tendon reflexes may be normal or brisk when pyramidal involvement is present in the complex phenotype.
Peripheral sensation is often relatively spared compared with several other autosomal recessive ataxias.
reference.pathophysiology: SYNE1 encodes nesprin-1, a giant spectrin-repeat protein of the outer nuclear membrane that, together with SUN-domain partners, forms the LINC complex physically coupling the nucleoskeleton to the cytoskeleton. Nesprin-1 is highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells and is also enriched at the neuromuscular junction, where it contributes to nuclear positioning and cytoskeletal organisation. Loss of functional nesprin-1 disrupts these structural links, and the resulting impairment of nuclear anchoring and cytoskeletal integrity is associated with degeneration of the cerebellar cortex, producing the characteristic ataxia. In the expanded phenotypes, additional involvement of motor neurons and brainstem structures is thought to reflect the wider distribution and function of nesprin-1, accounting for the pyramidal, lower motor neuron and bulbar features that can accompany the cerebellar syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia types 1 and 2
Sporadic adult-onset cerebellar ataxia and multiple system atrophy of cerebellar type
Motor neuron disease when lower and upper motor neuron signs dominate
Acquired ataxias including alcohol-related, gluten and paraneoplastic causes
additionalInvestigations: SYNE1 sequencing accounting for its very large size, or exome/recessive ataxia panel
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to assess neuropathy and motor neuron involvement
Creatine kinase where muscle or neuromuscular junction involvement is suspected
Screening for acquired causes of ataxia
Cognitive assessment where a complex multisystem phenotype is suspected
redFlags: Emergence of prominent lower motor neuron or bulbar signs suggesting motor neuron involvement
Rapid deterioration atypical for the usually slow cerebellar course
reference.prognosis: The disorder is usually slowly progressive with relatively preserved lifespan, particularly in the pure cerebellar form. Complex multisystem forms with motor neuron involvement may carry greater disability.
pitfalls: Assuming SYNE1 ataxia is always a pure cerebellar syndrome, when motor neuron and brainstem involvement can occur.
Missing the diagnosis because the very large gene poses technical sequencing challenges.
Mistaking complex SYNE1 phenotypes for primary motor neuron disease.
Assuming the disorder is confined to French-Canadian populations, when it is reported worldwide.
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so care is supportive and directed at symptoms
Provide physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain gait, balance and function, with mobility aids and falls prevention
Offer speech and language therapy for dysarthria and assessment of swallowing safety
Manage features of the expanded phenotype such as spasticity and lower motor neuron involvement symptomatically
Monitor for progression of swallowing, respiratory and motor-neuron complications over time
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive inheritance
Coordinate long-term care through a neurology-led multidisciplinary ataxia service
